notes: Ruling slot 22 = Military Directorate (de Souza, Kouandété, Sinzogan) formed after the 10 Dec 1969 coup. Slot 13 holds Maga's RDD as the strongest civilian bloc (no formal coalition existed). Apithy's PRD in 20 as Porto-Novo regional populism; Ahomadégbé's UDD in 18 (African socialism, RDA lineage). Parties were banned since 1965 and revive for the March 1970 elections.

0.name: Les Soglistes
0.text:
Les Soglistes are the officers and pro-French notables who remain loyal to General Christophe Soglo, who seized power in 1965 and was toppled by the junior officers of Major Maurice Kouandété in December 1967. Soglo lives in retirement, but his followers keep their posts in the gendarmerie, the ministries and the French cooperation offices.

They want a firm presidential regime under a senior officer, close defence ties with Paris and loyal membership of the Conseil de l'Entente around Félix Houphouët-Boigny. Their strength lies in the confidence of the French embassy and in older officers who resent the political adventures of the younger cadres.

1.name: Archidiocèse de Cotonou
1.text:
The Archdiocese of Cotonou heads the Catholic Church of Dahomey, one of the most Catholic societies of French West Africa and the training ground of much of its civil service. Archbishop Bernardin Gantin, the first African to lead the see, guides a clergy and a network of mission schools that formed most of the southern elite.

The Church preaches social peace, civilian government and reconciliation between the feuding regional leaders, and it stands firmly with the Western world against Marxist ideas in the student movement. Its leverage lies in its schools, its press and the moral authority it holds over Cotonou's teachers, clerks and officers.

2.name: Les Zinsouistes
2.text:
Les Zinsouistes are the civilian technocrats who served President Émile Derlin Zinsou, the physician and diplomat installed by the army in July 1968 and overthrown by Lieutenant-Colonel Maurice Kouandété on 10 December 1969. Stripped of office, Zinsou intends to stand in the elections the Military Directorate has promised for March 1970.

They stand for budget discipline, an end to political strikes, tax reform and an administration run by competence rather than regional loyalty. Close to Paris and to Western donors, they draw support from senior civil servants, Cotonou professionals and businessmen weary of the endless rivalry between Maga, Apithy and Ahomadégbé.

3.name: Union Générale des Travailleurs du Dahomey
3.native_full: Union Générale des Travailleurs du Dahomey
3.text:
The General Union of Dahomeyan Workers is the main trade union centre of Dahomey, grouping teachers, civil servants, dockers and railwaymen. Its general strikes helped bring down Hubert Maga in 1963 and repeatedly shook the governments that followed, and in January 1970 it watches the new Military Directorate with suspicion.

The union demands an end to wage cuts and special levies, respect for trade union freedom and a return to elected civilian rule. It keeps its distance from Moscow while working with Western-funded labour programmes. Its leverage lies in Cotonou and Porto-Novo, where a strike of public servants can paralyse the state within days.

4.name: Les Cercles marxistes
4.text:
Les Cercles marxistes are small clandestine study groups of teachers, students returned from Eastern Europe and young trade unionists in Cotonou and Porto-Novo. They read Lenin and the publications of the French Communist Party and keep discreet contacts with Soviet and East German diplomats in the region.

They denounce the regional barons and the officer cliques alike as servants of French neo-colonialism, and call for a vanguard party, nationalisation of the port and the banks, and alliance with the Soviet Union. With no legal existence, they work through union branches and school associations, waiting for a crisis that opens the door to revolution.

5.name: Union Générale des Étudiants et Élèves du Dahomey
5.english: General Union of Students and Pupils of Dahomey
5.native_full: Union Générale des Étudiants et Élèves du Dahomey
5.text:
The General Union of Students and Pupils of Dahomey unites secondary pupils and university students, the most restless constituency in the country. Its members spent 1969 in strikes and protests, and they greet the December coup with open contempt, regarding all three regional leaders as relics of the colonial era.

Radicalised by the events of 1968 in Paris and Dakar, its activists embrace anti-imperialism, Third World revolution and a sweeping purge of the old political class. They reject both the officers and the parties and call for popular power. Their leverage is the street: school strikes and demonstrations in Cotonou can force any government onto the defensive.

6.name: Les Vodunon
6.text:
Les Vodunon are the priests and dignitaries of the vodun cults of southern Dahomey, from the python temple of Ouidah to the convents of Abomey and the lagoon country. Marginalised by missionaries, colonial schooling and modern administration, they remain the guardians of ritual life for much of the rural south.

They defend ancestral custom against Catholic evangelism, Western education and the urban ways of the évolués, and look with sympathy on any authority that rejects French tutelage. Their influence runs through families, lineages and village councils, and no politician from the south can win Abomey or Ouidah without at least their quiet blessing.

7.name: Les Jeunes Cadres
7.text:
Les Jeunes Cadres are the junior officers who overthrew General Soglo in December 1967 under Major Maurice Kouandété, installed Zinsou, and then removed him on 10 December 1969. Kouandété, now a lieutenant-colonel, sits in the Military Directorate but resents that the army command placed Paul-Émile de Souza above him.

They see themselves as the cleansing force of the nation, impatient with the old politicians, suspicious of French advisers and drawn to the radical military regimes of Algeria and Egypt. Their base is the younger officer corps and northern soldiers loyal to Kouandété, and their weapon is the coup itself, which they have used twice in two years.

8.name: Communauté libanaise de Cotonou
8.text:
The Lebanese community of Cotonou is a close-knit commercial diaspora, largely Shia from southern Lebanon, that dominates import trade, textiles and retail in the capital and the towns of the south. Its families arrived in the colonial period and keep strong ties with Tyre, Nabatieh and Beirut.

Its elders follow the reformist line of Imam Musa al-Sadr, combining Shia identity with civic engagement, charity and good relations with the authorities of the day. Avoiding open politics, the community uses credit, employment and discreet donations to protect its business, and it can make or break a trader's fortunes in Cotonou's markets.

9.name: Le Cercle de Najaf
9.text:
Le Cercle de Najaf is a small group of devout Lebanese Shia merchants and their sons in Cotonou who look to the senior clergy of Najaf rather than to the community's accommodating elders. They gather in private prayer rooms, collect religious dues for their marja' and send young men to study in Iraq.

They hold that the community must live by religious law under clerical guidance and reject the secular habits of Western-educated Lebanese youth. Their numbers are tiny, but their piety earns them respect in the souk, and their links to Najaf give them a voice in the wider transnational Shia network.

10.name: Communauté musulmane de Porto-Novo
10.text:
The Muslim Community of Porto-Novo is the oldest Islamic establishment in southern Dahomey, centred on the great mosque of the capital built in the Afro-Brazilian style. Yoruba and Afro-Brazilian Muslim families, imams and Quranic teachers lead it, alongside the Muslim notables of the northern towns of Djougou, Parakou and Kandi.

The community preaches loyalty to the lawful authorities, the peaceful practice of Islam and the protection of Muslim schools, pilgrimage arrangements and family law. It avoids confrontation with the Catholic elite and seeks patronage from whoever governs. Its leverage lies in Friday sermons, trading networks and the votes of a cohesive minority.

11.name: Les Talibés du Nord
11.text:
Les Talibés du Nord are itinerant preachers and their Quranic students moving between Kandi, Malanville and the markets of northern Nigeria and Niger. Shaped by the memory of the Sokoto Caliphate and the jihad of Usman dan Fodio, they denounce the secular state inherited from France.

They preach that only a reborn caliphate under Islamic law can end corruption, Christian domination of the state and the moral decay of the towns. Harassed by local chiefs and ignored by Cotonou, they recruit among poor pupils and seasonal migrants, a fringe that could grow if hardship and disorder in the north deepen.

12.name: Les Arabisants
12.text:
Les Arabisants are young Dahomeyan Muslims who studied Arabic and theology in Cairo, at al-Azhar, or in Sudan and Saudi Arabia, and returned to find themselves shut out of a French-speaking administration. They teach in modern madrasas in Porto-Novo and Parakou and debate in small Muslim associations.

They want Islam to shape public morality and education, call for Arabic-language schooling and state recognition of Muslim diplomas, and reject both Marxism and Western permissiveness. Reformist rather than revolutionary, they admire the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood's call for renewal, and their influence grows among educated Muslim youth frustrated by the old notables.

13.name: Rassemblement Démocratique Dahoméen
13.text:
The Dahomeyan Democratic Rally is the political machine of Hubert Maga, first president of Dahomey from 1960 until his overthrow in 1963, and the voice of the north. Banned with all parties since 1965, its network of chiefs, teachers and Bariba and Dendi notables remains intact, and Maga, in exile, is preparing his return for the elections the Directorate has promised.

The RDD stands for northern equality, a strong presidency and pragmatic neutrality abroad combined with continuing French aid. Its leverage is the solid bloc vote of Borgou and Atakora, which makes Maga indispensable to any settlement between the regions.

14.name: La Chefferie du Borgou
14.text:
La Chefferie du Borgou is the network of Bariba princely houses headed by the king of Nikki, whose cavalry aristocracy ruled the north before the French conquest. The chiefs keep judicial and ceremonial authority over villages, Fulani herders and markets across the region.

Conservative and deeply attached to hierarchy, land rights and court tradition, they distrust the southern elite and the radical students alike, and demand a fair share of state posts for the north. They broker Maga's vote at village level and expect in return respect for their status, a voice in local administration and protection against land reform.

15.name: Chambre de Commerce et d'Industrie du Dahomey
15.english: Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Dahomey
15.native_full: Chambre de Commerce et d'Industrie du Dahomey
15.text:
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Dahomey speaks for the import-export houses, French trading firms and Dahomeyan merchants who run the port of Cotonou and the re-export trade with Nigeria and Niger. Its members finance politicians across the regional divide and pay much of the state's customs revenue.

They want order, low taxes on trade, a stable CFA franc and an end to the strikes that close the port. They prefer Western partners and French banking ties, and quietly fund whichever leader promises calm. Their leverage is economic: a slowdown at the port drains the treasury within weeks.

16.name: Les Revendeuses de Dantokpa
16.text:
Les Revendeuses de Dantokpa are the powerful market women of Cotonou's great market on the lagoon, who control the wholesale trade in cloth, foodstuffs and goods moved across the Nigerian border. Organised in rotating credit groups and trade associations, they handle fortunes in cash outside any bank.

They demand freedom of trade, low market fees and an end to police harassment, and loathe price controls and customs zeal. They fund politicians who leave them alone, mobilise crowds when taxes rise and can starve the city of goods if provoked. Their libertarian instinct is practical rather than ideological, but it is fierce.

17.name: Les Gardiens de la Pendjari
17.text:
Les Gardiens de la Pendjari are the foresters, wildlife wardens and hunters' associations of the Atakora who guard the Pendjari and W reserves, among the richest wildlife areas of West Africa. Supported by French and international conservation experts, they confront poaching, bush fires and land clearing.

They call for protecting forests, savannah and river valleys, sustainable hunting and the defence of the palm groves and lagoons of the south against overexploitation. Small and technical, they hold influence through the forestry service, foreign aid projects and the traditional hunters' brotherhoods, whose knowledge of the bush is respected in every northern village.

18.name: Union Démocratique Dahoméenne
18.text:
The Dahomeyan Democratic Union is the party of Justin Ahomadégbé, dentist, former head of government and scion of a princely lineage of Abomey, whose base lies among the Fon of the centre and south. Founded in 1956 and linked to the RDA, it has been banned since 1965, and Ahomadégbé now prepares his comeback for the coming elections.

The UDD speaks for teachers, unionists and the Fon heartland, combining African socialism with fierce rivalry toward Maga. It favours a strong state role in the economy, ties to radical African governments and independence from French tutelage. Its leverage is a disciplined southern vote and close links with the unions.

19.name: Fédération des Étudiants d'Afrique Noire en France
19.english: Federation of Black African Students in France
19.native_full: Fédération des Étudiants d'Afrique Noire en France
19.text:
The Federation of Black African Students in France gathers African students in French universities, and its Dahomeyan section is among its most militant. In January 1970 it sits at the heart of the post-1968 Latin Quarter left, where Maoist and Third-Worldist ideas dominate its congresses.

The Dahomeyan militants condemn the military regime, the regional barons and French neo-colonialism alike, and look to China, Vietnam and guerrilla struggle as models for national liberation. They want a people's democracy free of both superpowers' tutelage. Their influence reaches home through returning graduates, student newspapers and contacts with the radical wing of the school union.
19.wiki: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France

20.name: Parti Républicain du Dahomey
20.text:
The Republican Party of Dahomey is the vehicle of Sourou-Migan Apithy, the veteran deputy of Porto-Novo who served as president from 1964 until the army removed him in 1965. Banned with all parties, it survives as a network of Goun and Yoruba notables, merchants and chiefs in the old capital and the Ouémé valley.

The PRD is a regional populist machine: it promises Porto-Novo its due against Cotonou, Abomey and the north, defends local commerce and plays on fears of Fon domination. Apithy, pro-French and supremely flexible, uses the Ouémé's solid vote to make himself the arbiter of every three-way contest.

21.name: Ordre et Nation
21.text:
Ordre et Nation is a clique of hard-line officers and gendarmes who believe that the repeated coups since 1963 prove civilians unfit to rule. They despise the regional bosses, the unions and the students, and talk openly of a permanent military state.

They want a single national movement under the army, a disciplined youth militia, the outlawing of strikes and the suppression of regional and ethnic parties in the name of one Dahomeyan nation. Small but armed, they recruit among paratroopers and gendarmerie units around Cotonou, and see the elections planned for March as a dangerous step backwards.

22.name: Directoire militaire
22.text:
The Military Directorate has ruled Dahomey since 13 December 1969, three days after Lieutenant-Colonel Maurice Kouandété ousted President Zinsou. Unwilling to accept Kouandété as head of state, the army command imposed a triumvirate chaired by Lieutenant-Colonel Paul-Émile de Souza, with Kouandété and Lieutenant-Colonel Benoît Sinzogan.

The Directorate presents itself as a caretaker: it promises presidential elections for March 1970 and open competition between Maga, Apithy, Ahomadégbé and Zinsou. In practice the officer corps remains the final arbiter of power, divided by regional loyalties but united in its claim to save the nation from chaos.

23.name: Cour royale d'Abomey
23.text:
The Royal Court of Abomey preserves the heritage of the kingdom of Dahomey, whose kings ruled the Fon plateau until the French conquest of 1892–1894. The royal family, its councils and the palace dignitaries still keep the rites of the dynasty and command respect across the Fon heartland.

The court seeks recognition of traditional authority, protection of the palaces and royal cults, and a say in local justice and land. It distrusts northern dominance and leans toward Ahomadégbé, himself of princely Abomey descent. Its leverage is symbolic but real: royal favour still sways thousands of votes on the plateau.
